01.01.summary: This chapter explains how water's molecular structure—polar covalent bonds and bent geometry—creates the hydrogen bonding network responsible for cohesion, adhesion, surface tension, and its role as the universal solvent. It also covers how pH and buffer systems affect enzyme function through protonation of amino acid R groups.
keyConcepts: Electronegativity difference between oxygen (3.44) and hydrogen (2.20) creates polar covalent bonds
Bent molecular geometry (104.5°) produces a permanent dipole moment
Hydrogen bonds form between water molecules (not within them), each molecule can form up to four
Cohesion: hydrogen bonding between water molecules creates surface tension
Adhesion: hydrogen bonding between water and polar surfaces (e.g., cellulose hydroxyl groups)
Transpiration-cohesion-tension mechanism drives water transport in xylem
Hydration shells form around ions when water dissolves ionic compounds
Nonpolar molecules are excluded from aqueous solution due to water's polarity
pH measures H+ concentration and affects enzyme tertiary structure via R group protonation
Buffer systems resist pH change through reversible acceptance and release of H+ ions
topics: Water's bent molecular geometry and dipole moment
Hydrogen bonding network in liquid water
examTips: Hydrogen bonds hold water molecules to each other; covalent bonds hold atoms within a single water molecule—confusing these is a common FRQ error.
Xylem water transport is driven by cohesion and adhesion (transpiration pull), not osmosis—osmosis only applies when water crosses a selectively permeable membrane.

01.02.summary: This chapter explains why carbon's four valence electrons make it uniquely suited for biological molecules, covering how structural formulas reveal molecular behavior that molecular formulas cannot. It also identifies the six major functional groups and demonstrates how structural isomers with identical molecular formulas can exhibit entirely different biological properties.
keyConcepts: Carbon's four valence electrons enable four simultaneous covalent bonds
Tetrahedral geometry (109.5°) of carbon single bonds vs. planar geometry of double bonds
Hydrocarbon skeleton as nonpolar, stable backbone
Molecular formula vs. structural formula distinction
Structural isomers: same molecular formula, different atomic arrangement, different properties
Hydroxyl group (–OH): polar, hydrophilic, hydrogen bonding
Carbonyl group (C=O): aldehyde (terminal) vs. ketone (interior)
Carboxyl group (–COOH): acidic, proton donor, present in amino acids
Amino group (–NH2): basic, present in amino acids
Glucose vs. fructose as structural isomers (C6H12O6)
Butane vs. isobutane as structural isomers (C4H10)
Silicon vs. carbon: why carbon is biologically necessary
examTips: When asked why carbon is central to life, always reference its four valence electrons and ability to form four covalent bonds—never cite abundance or vague terms like 'building block'

When two molecules share the same molecular formula but have different properties, the answer always involves structural differences: functional group position, branching, or double bond location—never assume same formula means same behavior

01.03.summary: This chapter examines carbohydrates at the molecular level, tracing how monosaccharide ring geometry (alpha vs. beta glucose) determines the type of glycosidic linkage formed during dehydration synthesis and ultimately the shape and function of polysaccharides. It connects structural differences between starch, glycogen, and cellulose to their distinct biological roles using enzyme specificity and hydrogen bonding as the mechanistic explanations.
keyConcepts: Monosaccharide ring structure and anomeric carbon orientation
Alpha vs. beta glucose configuration
Dehydration synthesis and hydrolysis of glycosidic linkages
Alpha 1,4 glycosidic linkages produce helical, curved chains
Beta 1,4 glycosidic linkages produce straight chains
Alpha 1,6 glycosidic linkages create branch points
Enzyme specificity for alpha vs. beta linkages
Starch (amylose and amylopectin) as plant energy storage
Glycogen as animal energy storage with frequent branching
Hydrogen bonding between cellulose chains provides tensile strength
topics: Monosaccharide structure and the anomeric carbon
examTips: For free-response questions on starch vs. cellulose, go beyond naming alpha/beta linkages—explicitly trace the mechanism from bond geometry → chain shape (helix vs. straight) → biological function (energy storage vs. structural support) to earn full credit.
Remember the directional logic for reactions: dehydration synthesis removes water to BUILD glycosidic bonds, while hydrolysis adds water to BREAK them—distractors often reverse these.

01.04.summary: This chapter explains how lipid structure—particularly fatty acid saturation, cholesterol content, and phospholipid arrangement—determines membrane fluidity and function across temperature extremes. It also covers the entropy-driven hydrophobic effect as the thermodynamic basis for spontaneous bilayer self-assembly and contrasts lipid-soluble versus water-soluble hormone signaling pathways.
keyConcepts: Saturated fatty acids have straight chains that pack tightly, increasing membrane rigidity via maximized van der Waals interactions
Unsaturated fatty acids have cis double bond kinks (~30°) that prevent tight packing, increasing membrane fluidity
Polyunsaturated fatty acids create multiple kinks causing greater disruption to molecular packing than monounsaturated fatty acids
Organisms regulate saturated-to-unsaturated fatty acid ratios to maintain optimal membrane fluidity across temperature environments
The hydrophobic effect is entropy-driven: water excludes nonpolar tails to avoid low-entropy clathrate cage formation, releasing water molecules to maximize system entropy
Phospholipids are amphipathic molecules whose dual nature drives spontaneous bilayer self-assembly without energy input

Cholesterol acts as a membrane fluidity buffer: its rigid ring structure restricts tail movement at high temperatures (decreasing fluidity) and interrupts tight packing at low temperatures (preventing rigidity)
Lipid-soluble hormones cross the phospholipid bilayer directly; water-soluble hormones cannot and must bind surface receptors
Clathrate structures are ordered water cages around nonpolar surfaces that represent decreased entropy and are thermodynamically unfavorable
topics: Fatty acid saturation and hydrocarbon chain geometry
Molecular packing and van der Waals interactions in membranes
Membrane fluidity regulation in response to temperature
Amphipathic molecule behavior in aqueous environments
Cholesterol structure and temperature-dependent buffering of fluidity
Fluid mosaic model of membrane structure
Omega-3 and omega-6 fatty acid packing geometry
examTips: When predicting membrane composition for organisms in cold environments, always explain the mechanism: unsaturated fatty acid kinks physically prevent tight molecular alignment, not just that they 'increase fluidity'

Cholesterol is a fluidity BUFFER, not a simple fluidity enhancer—at high temperatures it decreases fluidity by restraining tail movement; at low temperatures it increases fluidity by preventing tight packing; always specify the temperature context

The driving force for bilayer formation is water entropy maximization (release of clathrate-ordered water), NOT attraction between lipids—distractor answers often cite hydrophobic attraction or inter-lipid hydrogen bonding

01.05.summary: This chapter explains the four hierarchical levels of protein structure—primary, secondary, tertiary, and quaternary—and the specific bonds and forces that stabilize each level. It also covers how denaturation disrupts protein function by breaking non-covalent interactions while preserving the covalent peptide bonds of primary structure.
keyConcepts: Primary structure: linear amino acid sequence held by covalent peptide bonds
Secondary structure: alpha helices and beta-pleated sheets stabilized by backbone hydrogen bonds
Tertiary structure: 3D shape from R-group interactions (hydrophobic effect, ionic bonds, hydrogen bonds, van der Waals, disulfide bridges)
Quaternary structure: multiple polypeptide subunits held by non-covalent forces
Denaturation: loss of secondary/tertiary/quaternary structure without breaking peptide bonds
Disulfide bridges as covalent stabilizers of tertiary structure
Hydrophobic effect driving interior burial of nonpolar R-groups
Heat, pH, and other environmental factors as denaturing agents
topics: Peptide bond formation via dehydration synthesis
Disulfide bridge formation between cysteine residues
Enzyme active site geometry and tertiary structure
Effects of mutations, pH changes, and temperature on protein function
examTips: Peptide bonds stabilize ONLY primary structure; hydrogen bonds stabilize secondary structure (backbone) and contribute to tertiary/quaternary (R-groups)—confusing these is a common point-losing mistake.
Denaturation does NOT break peptide bonds or separate amino acids; it only disrupts non-covalent interactions at secondary, tertiary, and quaternary levels, leaving primary structure intact.

01.06.summary: This chapter covers the structure and function of nucleic acids, focusing on how nucleotide chemistry determines strand directionality, how complementary base pairing stabilizes the double helix, and how three types of RNA execute the central dogma. Students learn to apply these principles to solve AP exam problems involving replication, transcription, and sequence determination.
keyConcepts: Nucleotide structure: pentose sugar, phosphate group at 5' carbon, nitrogenous base at 1' carbon
Phosphodiester bond formation and 5' to 3' strand directionality
DNA polymerase and RNA polymerase require a free 3' hydroxyl group for synthesis
Deoxyribose vs. ribose: the 2' OH makes RNA less stable than DNA
Purines (adenine, guanine) vs. pyrimidines (cytosine, thymine, uracil)
Complementary base pairing: A-T (2 hydrogen bonds), G-C (3 hydrogen bonds)
Antiparallel orientation of double helix strands
G-C content determines melting temperature (~0.4°C per 1% G-C)
Chargaff's rules: [A]=[T] and [G]=[C] in double-stranded DNA
Leading strand vs. lagging strand; Okazaki fragments on lagging strand
Central dogma: DNA → RNA → Protein
mRNA carries genetic code from nucleus to ribosome
Template strand (read 3'→5') vs. coding strand (same sequence as mRNA)
Three RNA types: mRNA, tRNA, rRNA with distinct mechanistic roles
topics: Deoxyribose vs. ribose and chemical stability
DNA thermal stability and melting temperature
G-C content and PCR primer design
Transcription: template strand vs. coding strand
Types of RNA and their roles in gene expression
examTips: When writing a complementary strand from a template, always identify the 3' end of the template first, start your new strand at its 5' end opposite that 3' end, and write toward your own 3' end — wrong polarity costs points on FRQs even with correct bases.

G-C pairs are more stable than A-T pairs because of three vs. two hydrogen bonds — not because of covalent bonds or base size; use this to reason about melting temperature and PCR annealing temperature questions.

01.07.summary: This chapter explains how enzymes lower activation energy by stabilizing the transition state through induced fit, and quantifies enzyme behavior using Michaelis-Menten kinetics including Km and Vmax. It also covers competitive and noncompetitive inhibition, allosteric/feedback regulation, and the effects of environmental factors on enzyme structure and function.
keyConcepts: Activation energy (Ea) and transition state stabilization
Induced fit model of enzyme-substrate interaction
Active site structure and catalytic mechanism
Michaelis-Menten kinetics: Vmax and Km
Enzyme-substrate affinity as inverse of Km
Competitive inhibition: active site binding, increased apparent Km, unchanged Vmax
Noncompetitive inhibition: allosteric site binding, decreased Vmax, unchanged Km
Allosteric regulation and feedback inhibition
Environmental effects on enzyme conformation and activity
topics: Reading Km and Vmax from graphs
Effects of temperature and pH on enzyme function
examTips: For FRQ full credit, do not just state enzymes lower Ea—explain the mechanism: induced fit strains substrate bonds and positions catalytic residues to stabilize the transition state.

When analyzing Michaelis-Menten graphs, always identify both parameters: find the plateau for Vmax first, then locate half-Vmax on the y-axis and read the corresponding x-value for Km—competitive inhibition raises Km only, noncompetitive inhibition lowers Vmax only.

01.08.summary: This chapter covers the structure and function of the cell membrane, explaining how the amphipathic nature of phospholipids drives spontaneous bilayer formation and how the fluid mosaic model describes the dynamic arrangement of proteins and lipids. It also addresses membrane transport mechanisms—including passive and active transport, osmosis, and water potential—and analyzes how disruptions to membrane components affect cellular function.
keyConcepts: Amphipathic phospholipids and spontaneous bilayer formation driven by entropy
Hydrophobic core creating selective permeability
Cholesterol as a fluidity buffer in animal cell membranes
Fluid mosaic model: lateral phospholipid movement and protein distribution
Integral vs. peripheral membrane proteins
Transmembrane proteins, channel proteins, and carrier proteins
Aquaporins and ion channel selectivity filters
Glycocalyx: glycoproteins and glycolipids in cell recognition
Osmosis and water potential calculations
Passive transport vs. active transport relative to concentration gradients and energy requirements
Effects of transport protein disruption on cellular and organismal physiology
examTips: When explaining spontaneous bilayer formation, always reference entropy: removing hydrophobic tails from water increases entropy of surrounding water by eliminating the ordered hydration cage—do not simply say 'like dissolves like.'

Distinguish channel proteins (open hydrophilic tunnels, no energy required) from carrier proteins (conformational change required) and both from active transporters (require ATP, move against concentration gradient) when answering transport mechanism questions.

02.01.summary: This chapter explains the fundamental organizational difference between prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells, focusing on compartmentalization through membrane-bound organelles as the mechanistic basis for eukaryotic functional complexity. It covers how internal membranes enable incompatible reactions to occur simultaneously, how surface area-to-volume ratio constrains cell size, and the structural evidence supporting endosymbiotic theory.
keyConcepts: Compartmentalization through membrane-bound organelles
Coupled vs. uncoupled transcription and translation
Post-transcriptional modification (5' capping, poly-A tail, intron splicing)
Nuclear envelope as physical separator of transcription and translation
Alternative splicing enabled by nuclear compartmentalization
Surface area-to-volume ratio constraints on cell size
Distinct chemical microenvironments in organelles (lysosome pH ~5, peroxisomes, mitochondrial matrix)
Endosymbiotic theory and supporting structural/molecular evidence
Nucleoid region in prokaryotes
Organelle-specific transport proteins as active regulators
topics: RNA processing and nuclear envelope function
Surface area-to-volume ratio and cell size scaling
Plant vs. animal cell structural differences
examTips: On FRQs about post-transcriptional modification, go beyond 'eukaryotes have a nucleus'—explicitly state that the nuclear envelope physically separates transcription from translation, creating time and space for 5' capping, polyadenylation, and splicing before ribosomes access the mRNA.

When comparing prokaryotes and eukaryotes, frame the difference as a principle of organization (compartmentalization), not just a parts list—explain how membrane-bound organelles enable simultaneous incompatible reactions that would be mutually destructive in a shared cytoplasmic space.

02.02.summary: This chapter examines how organelle structure directly enables function, focusing on the endomembrane system's continuous protein processing pathway and the mitochondrion's cristae architecture that maximizes ATP synthesis capacity. Students learn to trace secretory proteins through ER, Golgi, and vesicle trafficking, and to explain why membrane compartmentalization evolved for energy conversion in mitochondria and chloroplasts.
keyConcepts: Endomembrane system as a continuous, directional membrane network (ER → Golgi → target)
Co-translational insertion of proteins into the ER lumen via signal sequences and translocon channels
Golgi cis-medial-trans compartmentalization and sequential protein modification (glycosylation, mannose-6-phosphate tagging)
Vesicle budding and fusion maintaining membrane continuity during exocytosis
Cristae folds increasing inner mitochondrial membrane surface area to concentrate ATP synthase complexes
Proton-motive force across the inner mitochondrial membrane driving oxidative phosphorylation
Matrix as site of citric acid cycle enzymes producing NADH and FADH2
Compartmentalization enabling electrochemical gradient formation essential for ATP synthesis
examTips: When a secretory pathway step is blocked on FRQs, identify both the site of protein accumulation AND which modification is prevented (e.g., blocking ER-to-Golgi vesicle fusion means proteins accumulate in ER-derived vesicles and never receive Golgi glycosylation or mannose-6-phosphate sorting).

For cristae questions, use the full mechanistic chain: cristae folds → increased inner membrane surface area → more ATP synthase complexes embedded → higher rate of proton flow through ATP synthase → increased ATP production rate; never state that folds 'increase ATP' without explaining the mechanism.

02.03.summary: This chapter examines the three cytoskeletal filament systems—microtubules, microfilaments, and intermediate filaments—comparing their molecular composition, structural properties, and distinct cellular functions. It then explores how microtubule polarity governs motor protein directionality, how dynamic instability drives chromosome segregation, and how actin-myosin interactions produce cytokinetic force.
keyConcepts: Microtubules (25 nm) are hollow tubes of alpha/beta tubulin heterodimers arranged in 13 protofilaments
Microfilaments (7 nm) are solid F-actin double helices concentrated in the cell cortex
Intermediate filaments (10 nm) are rope-like fibrous protein assemblies providing tensile strength without active movement
Microtubule plus ends (beta tubulin exposed) grow faster and point toward the cell periphery; minus ends anchor at the centrosome
Kinesin is a plus-end-directed motor transporting cargo outward; dynein is a minus-end-directed motor transporting cargo inward
Motor proteins use ATP hydrolysis for cyclic conformational changes to walk along microtubule tracks
Dynamic instability: microtubules alternate between growth and rapid shrinkage, and depolymerization drives chromosome segregation during anaphase
Actin microfilaments and myosin generate contractile force at the cleavage furrow during animal cell cytokinesis
Intermediate filaments are the only cytoskeletal component that does not directly participate in cell movement
Drugs targeting tubulin or actin arrest cell division; intermediate filament disruption primarily affects tissue integrity
topics: Cytoskeletal filament types and molecular architecture
Intermediate filament composition and mechanical roles
Microtubule polarity and plus/minus end identity
Kinesin and dynein motor protein directionality
ATP hydrolysis mechanism of motor proteins
Dynamic instability and mitotic spindle function
Pharmacological and mutational disruption of cytoskeletal dynamics
examTips: Intermediate filaments are the ONLY cytoskeletal filament that is primarily structural and stable—any question about mechanical reinforcement, nuclear shape, or organelle anchoring without movement points to intermediate filaments, not microtubules or microfilaments.

Identify transport direction before selecting the motor protein: outward movement toward the plasma membrane = kinesin (plus-end directed); inward movement toward the nucleus/centrosome = dynein (minus-end directed).

02.04.summary: This chapter explains how a signal molecule's chemical properties determine whether it uses a surface or intracellular receptor, then details the complete GPCR signaling cascade including G-proteins, adenylyl cyclase, and cAMP as a second messenger. It also covers signal amplification, mutation consequences, and comparisons between lipid-soluble and lipid-insoluble signaling pathways.
keyConcepts: Chemistry rule: lipid solubility determines receptor location
Intracellular receptors for lipid-soluble signals (steroids, thyroid hormones)
Surface receptors for lipid-insoluble signals (protein hormones, neurotransmitters)
Hormone response elements and transcription factor activation
GPCR seven-transmembrane structure
G-protein heterotrimeric complex (alpha, beta, gamma subunits)
GDP-bound (inactive) vs. GTP-bound (active) G-protein states
Guanine nucleotide exchange factor (GEF) activity of activated GPCRs
Adenylyl cyclase and cAMP production from ATP
Intrinsic GTPase activity of alpha subunit for signal termination
Phosphodiesterase degradation of cAMP
Signal amplification through enzymatic cascades
Second messengers as intracellular signal relay molecules
Constitutive activation from GTPase-deficient mutations
examTips: When given an unfamiliar hormone, determine receptor location by chemistry: nonpolar/steroid = intracellular receptor; polar/protein/charged = surface receptor. Never assume all hormones work the same way.
G-protein activity is determined by bound nucleotide: GDP-bound = inactive, GTP-bound = active. A mutation preventing GTP hydrolysis causes constitutive activation, not inactivation.

02.05.summary: This chapter explains how molecules move across the plasma membrane through simple diffusion, channel proteins, carrier proteins, and bulk transport, emphasizing the role of molecular properties and protein mechanisms in determining transport pathways. It covers passive and active transport, ion channel selectivity, the Na+/K+ ATPase, and endocytosis/exocytosis as essential concepts for understanding cellular homeostasis.
keyConcepts: Hydrophobic core as a selective barrier to charged and polar molecules
Simple diffusion of small nonpolar and uncharged polar molecules down concentration gradients
Channel proteins forming hydrophilic pores for facilitated diffusion of ions and water
Selectivity filter mechanism in ion channels (chemical fit, not size exclusion)
Gated channels: voltage-gated, ligand-gated, and mechanically-gated
Leak channels and resting membrane potential
Carrier proteins using alternating access conformational changes
GLUT transporters as examples of carrier-mediated facilitated diffusion
Na+/K+ ATPase as a primary active transporter establishing electrochemical gradients
Secondary active transport powered by ion gradients
Endocytosis and exocytosis as bulk transport mechanisms bypassing bilayer crossing
Aquaporins as specialized water channels
topics: Active transport and the Na+/K+ ATPase
Transport protein inhibition and mutation consequences
examTips: Membrane permeability depends on molecular properties, not biological importance—steroid hormones (nonpolar) cross freely, but peptide hormones (polar/large) cannot.
Potassium channels exclude Na+ because Na+ is too SMALL to fit the selectivity filter's carbonyl oxygens, not because Na+ is larger—a common AP exam distractor gets this backwards.

02.06.summary: This chapter explains water potential (Ψ = Ψs + Ψp) as the governing force behind osmosis, detailing how to calculate and apply each component to predict water movement between compartments. It contrasts plant and animal cell responses to osmotic conditions, emphasizing how the plant cell wall generates turgor pressure to prevent lysis while animal cells are vulnerable to lysis and crenation.
keyConcepts: Water potential equation: Ψ = Ψs + Ψp
Solute potential (Ψs = −iCRT) is always zero or negative
Pressure potential (Ψp) is positive in walled cells, zero in animal cells
Water moves from higher to lower water potential
Turgor pressure in plant cells generated by rigid cell wall
Turgid, flaccid, and plasmolyzed states in plant cells
Lysis and hemolysis in animal cells in hypotonic solutions
Crenation in animal cells in hypertonic solutions
Isotonic, hypotonic, and hypertonic solution effects
Ionization constant (i) for solute dissociation in Ψs calculations
examTips: Always calculate total Ψ (Ψs + Ψp) for each compartment before predicting water movement direction—never compare solute potentials alone, as ignoring Ψp is a common free-response point-loss.

Lysis and crenation apply to animal cells; turgid, flaccid, and plasmolyzed apply to plant cells—if a question asks about a red blood cell becoming plasmolyzed, it is a distractor testing terminology distinctions.

02.07.summary: This chapter covers the three major types of cell communication—direct contact, local (paracrine and synaptic), and long-distance (endocrine) signaling—distinguishing each by mechanism and distance. It also addresses the structural basis of direct communication via gap junctions and plasmodesmata, the role of apoptosis as a programmed cellular response, and the consequences of disruptions in signaling pathways.
keyConcepts: Direct contact signaling via gap junctions and plasmodesmata
Gap junction structure: connexins, connexons, and pore size
Plasmodesmata structure: desmotubule, symplast, and plant cell wall channels
Paracrine signaling: local ligand diffusion without bloodstream involvement
Synaptic signaling: neurotransmitter release across the synaptic cleft
Endocrine signaling: hormone transport through the bloodstream to distant cells
Steroid hormones vs. peptide hormones and their mechanisms of action
Apoptosis as a programmed cell death response to signaling
Signal pathway disruption and mutation outcomes
examTips: Never use 'gap junction' and 'plasmodesmata' interchangeably—gap junctions are connexin-based protein channels in animals, while plasmodesmata are membrane-lined, desmotubule-containing channels through plant cell walls.
Do not classify every secreted ligand as endocrine signaling—if the signal acts on nearby or neighboring cells without traveling through the bloodstream, it is paracrine signaling, not endocrine.

02.08.summary: This chapter explains how homeostatic feedback loops maintain internal stability through three components—receptor, control center, and effector—that work together to detect and correct deviations from a set point. It distinguishes between negative feedback, which opposes the original stimulus to restore balance, and positive feedback, which amplifies the stimulus to drive rapid completion of physiological events.
keyConcepts: Homeostasis and set point maintenance
Three-component feedback loop: receptor, control center, effector
Negative feedback as a self-limiting stabilization mechanism
Positive feedback as an amplification mechanism
Thermoregulation via hypothalamic negative feedback
Blood glucose regulation via insulin and GLUT4
Role of pancreatic beta cells as receptor and effector
Hypothalamus as systemic control center
GLUT4 transporter insertion in response to insulin signaling
Disruption of feedback loop components and physiological consequences
topics: Control center comparison to set point
Thermoregulation: shivering, vasoconstriction, brown adipose tissue
Blood glucose regulation: insulin secretion and glucose uptake
Applying feedback loop analysis to novel scenarios
examTips: On FRQs, explicitly label all three components (receptor, control center, effector) for partial credit—even if uncertain about one, identify and label what you can using the format: receptor detects X, control center compares X to set point and initiates Y, effector performs Z.
For negative feedback MCQs involving unfamiliar systems, apply the opposition rule: a stimulus increase above set point must produce an effector response that decreases the variable, and vice versa.

03.01.summary: This chapter covers the thermodynamic principles governing biological reactions, focusing on Gibbs free energy (ΔG = ΔH − TΔS) as the determinant of reaction spontaneity in cellular systems. It explains how ATP coupling drives endergonic reactions, why cells comply with the Second Law of Thermodynamics, and how to distinguish thermodynamic spontaneity from kinetic reaction rate.
keyConcepts: Gibbs free energy (ΔG = ΔH − TΔS) and spontaneity
Exergonic vs. endergonic reactions
Exothermic vs. exergonic distinction
ATP hydrolysis as the primary cellular energy currency
ATP coupling via phosphorylated intermediates
Entropy and the Second Law of Thermodynamics
Cells as open systems that export entropy
Thermodynamic spontaneity vs. kinetic reaction rate
Effect of temperature on reaction favorability
Standard free energy change vs. actual cellular ΔG
topics: Gibbs free energy equation and its biological applications
Cellular respiration as an exergonic process
Protein synthesis as an endergonic process
Mechanism of ATP coupling in glutamine synthesis
Role of phosphorylated intermediates in coupled reactions
Entropy, disorder, and the Second Law
Enthalpy and entropy contributions to spontaneity
Activation energy and the spontaneity-rate distinction
examTips: Never equate spontaneous with fast—spontaneity means ΔG is negative (thermodynamic favorability), not that the reaction occurs quickly; high activation energy can make a spontaneous reaction extremely slow.

Never substitute exothermic for exergonic on free response; exergonic means ΔG < 0 (free energy), while exothermic means ΔH < 0 (heat)—a reaction can be exergonic and endothermic simultaneously if entropy increase is large enough.

03.02.summary: This chapter explains how ATP functions as the cell's energy currency, focusing on why hydrolysis releases energy through electrostatic repulsion relief and product stabilization rather than high-energy bonds. It covers the two mechanisms of ATP synthesis (substrate-level and oxidative phosphorylation), the proton motive force driving ATP synthase, and anaerobic ATP production via fermentation.
keyConcepts: ATP molecular structure: adenine, ribose, and three phosphate groups (alpha, beta, gamma)
Electrostatic repulsion among negatively charged phosphate groups as the source of ATP's free energy
ATP hydrolysis is exergonic (ΔG ≈ −30.5 kJ/mol) due to charge separation, resonance stabilization of Pi, and entropy increase
Energy coupling: direct mechanistic linkage of exergonic ATP hydrolysis to endergonic processes via phosphorylation
Phosphorylation-induced conformational changes enable cellular work (e.g., Na+/K+-ATPase)
Kinetic stability of ATP: slow spontaneous hydrolysis ensures controlled energy release
Substrate-level phosphorylation: direct phosphate transfer from high-energy intermediates (e.g., PEP) to ADP
Oxidative phosphorylation: ATP synthesis driven by the proton motive force across the inner mitochondrial membrane
ATP synthase rotation driven by proton gradient
Fermentation as an anaerobic strategy to regenerate NAD+ and sustain glycolytic ATP production
topics: Electrostatic repulsion and free energy of hydrolysis
Gibbs free energy and exergonic reactions
Na+/K+-ATPase as a model of coupled transport
Substrate-level phosphorylation in glycolysis and citric acid cycle
Oxidative phosphorylation and the electron transport chain
Proton motive force and ATP synthase
examTips: Never state that breaking the phosphate bond releases stored energy; instead explain that products (ADP + Pi) are more stable than ATP due to relief of electrostatic repulsion, resonance stabilization of Pi, and increased entropy.

When explaining ATP-driven endergonic processes, describe the full coupling mechanism: ATP transfers a phosphate to the substrate/protein, the phosphorylated intermediate undergoes a conformational change, and this change performs the work—simply saying 'ATP provides energy' is insufficient for free response credit.

03.03.summary: This chapter covers glycolysis as the universal first stage of cellular respiration, detailing the investment phase (steps 1–5, costing 2 ATP) and the payoff phase (steps 6–10, yielding 4 ATP and 2 NADH) for a net gain of 2 ATP per glucose. It also addresses regulation by phosphofructokinase, substrate-level vs. oxidative phosphorylation, and the critical role of NAD+ regeneration when mitochondrial function is impaired.
keyConcepts: Investment phase: 2 ATP consumed to phosphorylate and destabilize glucose (steps 1–5)
Hexokinase catalyzes glucose → glucose-6-phosphate, trapping glucose in the cell
Phosphofructokinase (PFK) as the primary regulatory enzyme of glycolysis
Allosteric inhibition of PFK by ATP and citrate; activation by AMP and ADP
Aldolase cleaves fructose-1,6-bisphosphate into DHAP and glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate
Triose phosphate isomerase converts DHAP → G3P so both halves enter the payoff phase
Payoff phase: 4 ATP produced via substrate-level phosphorylation, net = 2 ATP per glucose
Substrate-level phosphorylation vs. oxidative phosphorylation
NADH produced in glycolysis; NAD+ must be regenerated for glycolysis to continue
Glycolytic rate increases when mitochondria are inhibited due to NAD+ regeneration via fermentation
examTips: FRQ rubrics require mechanistic explanation for ATP investment: phosphorylation by hexokinase and PFK destabilizes glucose and traps it in the cell—never say the investment is random.
When mitochondria are inhibited, glycolysis speeds up (not stops) because fermentation regenerates NAD+, allowing substrate-level phosphorylation to continue; only oxidative phosphorylation is lost.

03.04.summary: This chapter covers pyruvate oxidation in the mitochondrial matrix, where the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex converts pyruvate to acetyl-CoA, and the citric acid cycle, which completely oxidizes acetyl groups to CO2 while generating NADH, FADH2, and ATP. Together these pathways account for all six carbons from glucose as CO2 and produce the electron carriers that drive oxidative phosphorylation.
keyConcepts: Oxidative decarboxylation of pyruvate by the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex
Products of pyruvate oxidation: acetyl-CoA, NADH, CO2 (per pyruvate: 1 each; per glucose: 2 each)
Citric acid cycle (Krebs/TCA cycle) as a closed loop using oxaloacetate as recyclable scaffold
Per-turn citric acid cycle yield: 3 NADH, 1 FADH2, 1 ATP/GTP, 2 CO2
Per-glucose citric acid cycle yield: 6 NADH, 2 FADH2, 2 ATP, 4 CO2
Carbon accounting: 2 CO2 from pyruvate oxidation + 4 CO2 from citric acid cycle = 6 CO2 total per glucose
Substrate-level phosphorylation vs. electron carrier reduction in the citric acid cycle
Subcellular compartmentalization: glycolysis in cytoplasm, pyruvate oxidation and citric acid cycle in mitochondrial matrix
Succinate dehydrogenase as the only citric acid cycle enzyme embedded in the inner mitochondrial membrane
Allosteric regulation of pyruvate dehydrogenase by ATP, NADH, and acetyl-CoA
Anaplerotic reactions replenishing oxaloacetate to maintain cycle continuity
Irreversibility of pyruvate oxidation due to CO2 release
topics: Citric acid cycle steps and intermediates
Carbon atom fate through cellular respiration
GTP/ATP production via substrate-level phosphorylation in citric acid cycle
NADH and FADH2 production as electron carriers
examTips: Pyruvate oxidation occurs specifically in the mitochondrial matrix, not just 'in the mitochondria'; if mitochondrial transport is blocked, only glycolysis can proceed.
Memorize the CO2 tally: glycolysis = 0 CO2, pyruvate oxidation = 2 CO2, citric acid cycle = 4 CO2, totaling 6 CO2 per glucose to match all six original carbons.

03.05.summary: This chapter explains how the electron transport chain (Complexes I–IV) transfers electrons from NADH and FADH2 to oxygen, using released energy to pump protons into the intermembrane space and establish the gradient that drives ATP synthase. It also distinguishes the proton-pumping capacities of NADH versus FADH2 and analyzes how inhibitors or uncouplers disrupt ATP production.
keyConcepts: Electron transport chain architecture (Complexes I–IV)
Complex I (NADH dehydrogenase) pumps 4 protons per NADH
Complex II (succinate dehydrogenase) does not pump protons, explaining lower FADH2 ATP yield
Ubiquinone (Coenzyme Q) as mobile lipid-soluble electron carrier
Cytochrome c as mobile electron carrier between Complex III and IV
Complex III Q cycle pumps 4 protons
Complex IV reduces O2 to water and pumps 2–4 protons
Oxygen as terminal electron acceptor, not energy source
Chemiosmosis and the proton electrochemical gradient
ATP synthase couples proton flow to ADP phosphorylation
NADH yields ~2.5 ATP; FADH2 yields ~1.5 ATP
ETC inhibitors (e.g., cyanide) cause electron backup and halt ATP synthesis
Uncouplers dissipate proton gradient without ATP production
topics: Architecture of the electron transport chain
Proton pumping by Complexes I, III, and IV
Role of ubiquinone and cytochrome c as mobile carriers
Thermodynamic basis of electron flow through the ETC
Differential ATP yield of NADH vs. FADH2
Effects of ETC inhibitors on electron flow and ATP production
Electron backup caused by Complex IV inhibition (cyanide)
Comparison of aerobic vs. anaerobic ATP yield
examTips: NADH enters at Complex I (pumps 4 H+, ~2.5 ATP); FADH2 enters at Complex II (no proton pumping, ~1.5 ATP)—this distinction is a high-frequency AP exam target.

Oxygen does not provide energy; it accepts low-energy electrons at Complex IV to prevent electron backup—AP questions use words like 'burns' or 'provides energy' for oxygen to trap students holding a combustion model.

03.06.summary: This chapter explains fermentation as a NAD+ regeneration mechanism rather than an ATP-producing pathway, detailing how cells survive without oxygen by using pyruvate as an alternative electron acceptor. It compares lactic acid fermentation (direct one-step reduction of pyruvate to lactate) with ethanol fermentation (two-step decarboxylation then reduction), and quantifies the ATP yield difference between fermentation and aerobic respiration.
keyConcepts: Fermentation regenerates NAD+ to sustain glycolysis, not to produce ATP
NAD+ depletion halts glycolysis when oxygen is unavailable
Lactic acid fermentation: lactate dehydrogenase reduces pyruvate directly to lactate, no CO2 released
Ethanol fermentation: pyruvate decarboxylase removes CO2 to form acetaldehyde, then alcohol dehydrogenase reduces acetaldehyde to ethanol
Pyruvate serves as the electron acceptor in both fermentation pathways
Fermentation yields only 2 ATP per glucose (from glycolysis) vs. ~30-32 ATP via aerobic respiration
NADH oxidation back to NAD+ is the essential function of fermentation
Muscle fatigue linked to proton accumulation and pH decrease, not lactate itself
Saccharomyces cerevisiae performs ethanol fermentation; Lactobacillus performs lactic acid fermentation
topics: Pyruvate decarboxylase and alcohol dehydrogenase enzymes
ATP yield comparison: fermentation vs. aerobic respiration
Industrial and biological applications of fermentation
examTips: Never state fermentation produces ATP without oxygen — fermentation's sole purpose is NAD+ regeneration so glycolysis can continue producing ATP via substrate-level phosphorylation; this distinction is frequently tested on FRQs.

Distinguish the two pathways by CO2 release: lactic acid fermentation produces no CO2 (no decarboxylation), while ethanol fermentation releases CO2 when pyruvate is converted to acetaldehyde — gas bubbles in an experiment indicate ethanol fermentation.

03.07.summary: This chapter covers the light-dependent reactions of photosynthesis, focusing on the structural organization of the thylakoid membrane and the sequential flow of electrons from water through Photosystem II, the cytochrome b6f complex, and Photosystem I to produce NADPH and ATP. Students learn how the proton gradient is established by two distinct mechanisms and how chemiosmosis drives ATP synthesis, with emphasis on the specific chemical roles of P680 and P700.
keyConcepts: Thylakoid membrane architecture: lumen vs. stroma compartmentalization
Four major protein complexes: PSII, cytochrome b6f, PSI, ATP synthase
Z-scheme: linear electron flow from water to NADPH
P680 as the strongest biological oxidizing agent capable of water splitting
P700 re-energizes electrons for NADP+ reduction
Oxygen evolving complex and water splitting: 2H2O → 4H+ + 4e- + O2
Two mechanisms of proton gradient formation: water splitting at PSII lumen side and active proton pumping by cytochrome b6f
Chemiosmosis: proton return through ATP synthase drives ATP synthesis in the stroma
Mobile electron carriers: plastoquinone and plastocyanin
NADPH production via ferredoxin and NADP+ reductase on stromal side
topics: Role of oxygen as a byproduct of water splitting
Functional order of photosystems vs. discovery order
examTips: ATP is released into the stroma and NADPH is produced on the stromal side—saying 'in the chloroplast' is insufficient for free-response credit; specify thylakoid membrane (ATP synthase) and stromal face.

Photosystem II functions FIRST despite being numbered second; PSII must precede PSI because only P680+ is a strong enough oxidizing agent to extract electrons from water—P700+ cannot perform water oxidation.

03.08.summary: This chapter covers the three stages of the Calvin cycle—carbon fixation by RuBisCO, reduction of 3-PGA to G3P, and regeneration of RuBP—detailing the specific inputs, outputs, and energy requirements at each stage. It also addresses RuBisCO's dual carboxylase/oxygenase activity leading to photorespiration, and distinguishes C3, C4, and CAM photosynthetic pathways by their CO2 concentration mechanisms and first stable carbon products.
keyConcepts: RuBisCO catalyzes CO2 fixation: CO2 + RuBP → 2 molecules of 3-PGA
3-PGA is the first stable product of carbon fixation in C3 plants
Reduction stage: 3-PGA → 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate → G3P, consuming ATP and NADPH
G3P is the Calvin cycle output and precursor for glucose, amino acids, and lipids
RuBP regeneration: 5 G3P (15C) → 3 RuBP (15C), requires ATP
Stoichiometry: 3 CO2 fixed per cycle, 6 G3P produced, 1 net G3P exported, 5 recycled
Per CO2 fixed: 2 ATP and 2 NADPH consumed in reduction stage
RuBisCO oxygenase activity produces 2-phosphoglycolate, triggering photorespiration
Photorespiration consumes ATP, releases fixed CO2, and produces no usable sugar
C3 plants fix CO2 directly via RuBisCO; first stable product is 3-PGA (3 carbons)
C4 and CAM plants use CO2-concentrating mechanisms to reduce photorespiration
Calvin cycle location: stroma of the chloroplast
Light reactions supply ATP and NADPH consumed by the Calvin cycle
RuBP regeneration is the rate-limiting control point linking light reactions to carbon fixation
topics: ATP and NADPH consumption in the Calvin cycle
Coupling of light reactions to Calvin cycle
Radioactive carbon tracer experiments (Calvin cycle intermediates)
examTips: For FRQ credit on RuBisCO inefficiency, state TWO explicit points: (1) it is the sole entry point for atmospheric CO2 into organic carbon, and (2) its oxygenase activity produces 2-phosphoglycolate, triggering wasteful photorespiration—both require mechanism-level explanation.

Trace ATP and NADPH from their production site (thylakoid membranes via chemiosmosis and ferredoxin reduction) to their consumption site (stroma, reduction stage of Calvin cycle converting 3-PGA to G3P); also memorize per-CO2 costs: 3 ATP and 2 NADPH total per CO2 fixed across the full cycle.

03.09.summary: This chapter examines the relationship between cellular respiration and photosynthesis, emphasizing that they are not perfect opposites but simultaneous processes requiring careful rate accounting. Students learn to calculate true (gross) photosynthesis from gas exchange data, compare electron transport chain mechanisms in mitochondria and chloroplasts, and design experiments to distinguish apparent from true metabolic rates.
keyConcepts: True (gross) photosynthesis = apparent photosynthesis + respiration rate
Compensation point: light intensity where photosynthesis rate equals respiration rate, yielding zero net gas exchange
Apparent photosynthesis is always less than true photosynthesis due to simultaneous respiration
Chemiosmosis drives ATP synthesis in both mitochondria and chloroplasts via proton gradients
In mitochondria, protons accumulate in the intermembrane space; in chloroplasts, protons accumulate in the thylakoid lumen
Oxygen is the final electron acceptor in mitochondria; oxygen is a byproduct of water splitting in chloroplasts
Both processes operate simultaneously in photosynthetic cells containing both chloroplasts and mitochondria
Dark respiration rate remains relatively constant regardless of light conditions
Net gas exchange reflects the combined, simultaneous effects of photosynthesis and respiration
topics: Gas exchange calculations using oxygen and CO2 data
Electron transport chain comparison: chloroplasts vs. mitochondria
Proton gradient orientation in thylakoid lumen vs. intermembrane space
Experimental methods: oxygen probes, CO2 sensors, radioactive tracers
examTips: Never equate measured oxygen output in the light with true photosynthesis rate — always add the dark respiration rate to apparent photosynthesis to find gross photosynthesis.
Zero net gas exchange means the compensation point has been reached, NOT that photosynthesis has stopped; both processes are running at equal rates.

04.01.summary: This chapter explains the three-stage process of signal transduction—reception, transduction, and response—detailing how ligand binding causes receptor conformational changes, how phosphorylation cascades amplify signals exponentially, and how activated cascades produce fast cytoplasmic or slow gene expression responses. It also covers cell-specific signaling, second messengers, and the molecular mechanisms that terminate and reverse signaling.
keyConcepts: Ligand-receptor binding and conformational change
G protein-coupled receptors, receptor tyrosine kinases, and ion channel receptors
Phosphorylation cascades and signal amplification
Protein kinases and phosphatases
Second messengers (cAMP, calcium ions, IP3)
MAPK pathway
Fast cytoplasmic responses vs. slow gene expression responses
Signal termination and reversibility
Cell-specific responses through differential receptor expression
topics: Reception: ligand binding and receptor conformational change
Receptor types: GPCRs, RTKs, ion channel receptors
Slow transcriptional responses via gene expression
Receptor specificity and differential gene expression
examTips: Reception = ligand binding + conformational change only; any mention of phosphorylation or enzyme activation describes transduction—keep these stages strictly separate on FRQs.
To earn full credit for amplification questions, explicitly state the multiplicative mechanism: each kinase activates multiple copies of the next kinase, not just that 'the signal gets stronger.'

04.02.summary: This chapter covers the four phases of the cell cycle (G1, S, G2, M) and explains why each phase must precede the next based on molecular prerequisites. It also details the three major checkpoints (G1/S, G2/M, Spindle Assembly), cyclin-CDK regulation, and how mutations in tumor suppressors and proto-oncogenes lead to cancer.
keyConcepts: G1 phase: cell growth and growth factor integration
S phase: DNA replication and sister chromatid formation
G2 phase: DNA repair and mitotic protein synthesis
M phase: chromosome segregation and cytokinesis
G0 quiescent state
G1/S restriction point checkpoint
G2/M checkpoint: verifying complete and accurate DNA replication
Spindle Assembly Checkpoint: bipolar kinetochore attachment
Cyclin-CDK complexes and phosphorylation of target proteins
p53 tumor suppressor and p21 CDK inhibitor
ATM and ATR sensor kinases
Mitotic Checkpoint Complex and Anaphase Promoting Complex
Proto-oncogenes vs. tumor suppressors in cancer
DNA content vs. chromosome number distinction
topics: Cell cycle phases (G1, S, G2, M, G0)
Molecular events and prerequisites of each cell cycle phase
Cell cycle checkpoints and their specific functions
Growth factor signaling and receptor tyrosine kinases
Spindle microtubule assembly and chromosome segregation
examTips: DNA content doubles during S phase, but chromosome number stays constant until anaphase—a diploid human cell has 92 DNA molecules but still 46 chromosomes after S phase.

Each checkpoint monitors a distinct condition: G1/S checks cell size, nutrients, growth factors, and DNA integrity; G2/M checks for complete and accurate replication; the Spindle Assembly Checkpoint checks for bipolar kinetochore attachment—do not conflate them as all simply 'checking for DNA damage.'

04.03.summary: This chapter covers the molecular mechanisms of mitosis, focusing on chromosome structure after replication, spindle apparatus function, and the precise segregation of sister chromatids. It explains how kinetochore-microtubule interactions, motor proteins, and checkpoint mechanisms ensure accurate chromosome distribution to daughter cells.
keyConcepts: Sister chromatids vs. homologous chromosomes
Centromere and cohesin function in holding sister chromatids together
Chromosome number vs. chromatid number at different cell cycle stages
Mitotic spindle structure: kinetochore, polar, and astral microtubules
Amphitelic (bioriented) attachment of kinetochores to opposite spindle poles
Dynamic instability of microtubules
Force generation during anaphase via microtubule depolymerization
Kinesin and dynein motor protein roles in spindle function
Aurora B kinase error correction of improper kinetochore attachments
Separase cleavage of cohesin to trigger anaphase
Condensin-mediated chromosome condensation during prophase
Spindle assembly checkpoint (SAC) preventing premature anaphase
PMAT phases: prophase, prometaphase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase
topics: Mitotic spindle apparatus and microtubule types
examTips: Chromosome number changes only when centromeres separate at anaphase: a post-replication cell has 46 chromosomes (92 chromatids) until anaphase, when it briefly has 92 chromosomes before cytokinesis restores 46 per cell.

For free-response questions about anaphase chromosome movement, describe microtubule depolymerization at the kinetochore end with the kinetochore tracking the shrinking end—do not say a motor protein pulls the chromosome along a static microtubule track.

04.04.summary: This chapter covers the mechanics of meiosis, explaining how two sequential divisions reduce chromosome number and generate genetic diversity through crossing over and independent assortment. It also addresses meiotic errors leading to aneuploidy and connects genetic variation in gametes to evolutionary fitness.
keyConcepts: Meiosis I is the reductive division separating homologous chromosomes (2n to n); Meiosis II separates sister chromatids like mitosis
DNA content changes: 4C before meiosis, 2C after Meiosis I, 1C after Meiosis II
Synapsis and bivalent (tetrad) formation during Prophase I
Crossing over occurs between non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes during Prophase I
Chiasmata are visible sites of crossing over and hold homologs together until Anaphase I
SPO11 initiates programmed double-strand breaks to start recombination
Independent assortment generates 2^n chromosome combinations
Meiotic nondisjunction causes aneuploidy with predictable phenotypic consequences
Genetic diversity in gametes provides selective evolutionary advantages
topics: Architecture of Meiosis I vs. Meiosis II
Ploidy vs. DNA content (n vs. C values)
Evolutionary significance of meiotic genetic diversity
examTips: FRQ credit requires specifying that Meiosis I separates HOMOLOGOUS chromosomes (not just 'chromosomes') to cause ploidy reduction; Meiosis II separates SISTER CHROMATIDS.
When explaining crossing over, you must state it occurs between NON-SISTER chromatids of HOMOLOGOUS chromosomes during PROPHASE I — omitting any of these specifics loses points.

04.05.summary: This chapter explains how mutations in proto-oncogenes and tumor suppressor genes disrupt normal cell cycle control, leading to uncontrolled proliferation and cancer. It covers the molecular mechanisms of oncogene activation, the two-hit hypothesis for tumor suppressor inactivation, checkpoint failure, and metastasis.
keyConcepts: Proto-oncogenes encode normal growth-promoting proteins; oncogenes are mutated, constitutively active forms
Oncogene mutations are gain-of-function and dominant — one mutated allele is sufficient
Tumor suppressor mutations are loss-of-function and recessive — both alleles must be inactivated (two-hit hypothesis)
Ras protein cycles between GTP-bound (active) and GDP-bound (inactive) states to transduce growth signals
Rb protein sequesters E2F transcription factors to block G1/S transition until phosphorylated by cyclin D/CDK4
p53 acts as guardian of the genome, inducing p21-mediated arrest or BAX-mediated apoptosis in response to DNA damage
Cancer requires multiple mutations because redundant, independent checkpoint systems must all fail
Inherited cancer syndromes (e.g., Li-Fraumeni) arise when one allele is already mutated at birth, requiring only one somatic hit
G1/S checkpoint controlled by Rb pathway and p53; G2/M checkpoint controlled by ATM/ATR kinases
Loss of cell adhesion molecules contributes to metastasis by enabling cells to detach and invade distant tissues
examTips: Never describe a proto-oncogene as harmful — it is a normal gene; only the mutated oncogene form is oncogenic. Oncogenes are dominant (one hit), tumor suppressors are recessive (two hits); mixing these up is one of the most common AP exam errors.

For tumor suppressor questions, remember that one functional allele is sufficient for checkpoint control — inherited one-allele mutations create predisposition, not immediate cancer. Always connect p53 loss to failure of both arrest (via p21) and apoptosis (via BAX).

04.06.summary: This chapter explains apoptosis as a genetically programmed cell death mechanism that serves essential biological functions in development, immunity, and cancer prevention. It details the intrinsic (mitochondrial) and extrinsic (death receptor) pathways, the caspase cascade execution mechanism, and the consequences of apoptosis dysregulation.
keyConcepts: Apoptosis as adaptive programmed cell death, not pathology
Intrinsic pathway: BAX/BAK, MOMP, cytochrome c release, apoptosome, caspase-9
Extrinsic pathway: death receptors (Fas), FADD, DISC formation, caspase-8
Caspase cascade: procaspase zymogens activated by proteolytic cleavage
Bcl-2 family proteins (anti-apoptotic Bcl-2/Bcl-xL vs. pro-apoptotic BAX/BAK)
Neural pruning via apoptosis during brain development
Negative selection of self-reactive T cells in the thymus
Apoptotic body formation and phagocytosis without inflammation
Apoptosis dysregulation leading to cancer, autoimmunity, or developmental defects
Apoptosis vs. necrosis: ordered dismantling vs. inflammatory cell rupture
topics: Programmed cell death logic and biological rationale
Bcl-2 family proteins and apoptosis regulation
Developmental roles of apoptosis (digit formation, neural pruning)
Immune system apoptosis (negative selection, clonal contraction)
examTips: Apoptosis absence—not presence—causes disease; when a question describes cancer or autoimmunity, the answer is almost always that apoptosis failed to eliminate dangerous cells.

Match pathway components precisely: cytochrome c, apoptosome, and caspase-9 are intrinsic pathway only; Fas, FADD, DISC, and caspase-8 are extrinsic pathway only—placing cytochrome c in the extrinsic pathway is a common trap.

04.07.summary: This chapter explains the stem cell hierarchy from totipotent to pluripotent to multipotent cells, emphasizing that developmental potential is restricted through epigenetic commitment rather than gene loss. It details how differential gene expression via transcription factor networks and epigenetic mechanisms like DNA methylation and histone modification produce specialized cell types from identical genomes.
keyConcepts: Totipotency vs. pluripotency vs. multipotency
Extraembryonic tissue formation as the key distinction for totipotent cells
Blastocyst inner cell mass as source of pluripotent embryonic stem cells
Hematopoietic stem cells as a model of multipotency
Differential gene expression from identical genomes
Transcription factor networks and cell identity
Master regulatory transcription factors and feed-forward loops
DNA methylation at CpG dinucleotides silencing gene promoters
DNMT1 maintenance methylation ensuring heritable silencing
Histone modification altering chromatin accessibility
Epigenetic restriction as the molecular basis of developmental commitment
Reciprocal relationship between transcription factors and epigenetic marks
topics: Stem cell hierarchy and developmental potential
Totipotent, pluripotent, and multipotent stem cells
Blastocyst formation and inner cell mass
Heritable epigenetic marks across cell divisions
examTips: Totipotent cells are the only type that can form extraembryonic structures like the placenta; if a question mentions forming 'all body cell types,' both totipotent and pluripotent may seem correct, but only totipotent is accurate when extraembryonic tissues are involved.

Free response answers about why differentiated cells express different genes must include both transcription factors AND epigenetic mechanisms for full credit; stating that cells lost genes or have different DNA sequences earns zero credit.

04.08.summary: This chapter examines the structural and functional roles of cell junctions (tight junctions, desmosomes, and gap junctions) and extracellular matrix components (collagen, proteoglycans, fibronectin, laminin) in maintaining tissue integrity. It also explores how integrin signaling, contact inhibition, and disruption of these systems contribute to cancer metastasis.
keyConcepts: Tight junctions seal the paracellular pathway using claudin and occludin proteins
Desmosomes anchor intermediate filaments between adjacent cells via cadherin proteins for mechanical strength
Gap junctions create cytoplasmic continuity via connexon channels (6 connexin subunits each) for ion and small molecule transfer
Collagen triple helix structure resists tensile forces and is the dominant structural protein in connective tissue
Proteoglycans resist compression through negatively charged glycosaminoglycan chains that attract water
Fibronectin and laminin are adhesive glycoproteins that organize ECM and link it to cells
Integrins are transmembrane receptors that connect ECM to the intracellular cytoskeleton and activate signaling cascades
Contact inhibition stops normal cell proliferation when cells reach confluency; loss of contact inhibition is a hallmark of cancer
topics: Paracellular pathway and epithelial barrier function
Collagen structure, assembly, and tissue-specific organization
Fibronectin and laminin as adhesive glycoproteins
Contact inhibition and normal cell cycle control
Cancer metastasis and loss of junction/ECM integrity
examTips: Use functional clues to identify junction type: leakage between cells = tight junctions/claudins; blistering/tearing under stress = desmosomes/intermediate filaments; loss of electrical or chemical coordination = gap junctions/connexins
Do not confuse tight junctions (create barriers) with gap junctions (create passages); their functions are opposite even though both connect adjacent cells

05.01.summary: This chapter explains Mendelian genetics by connecting Mendel's Laws of Segregation and Independent Assortment to the physical behavior of chromosomes during meiosis I. Students learn to predict genotype and phenotype ratios using Punnett squares and probability rules, design test crosses, and distinguish descriptive laws from chromosomal mechanisms.
keyConcepts: Law of Segregation: homologous chromosome separation at anaphase I causes each gamete to receive only one allele
Law of Independent Assortment: random orientation of chromosome pairs at metaphase I produces independent sorting of alleles on different chromosomes
Monohybrid cross (Bb x Bb) yields 1:2:1 genotypic ratio and 3:1 phenotypic ratio
Dihybrid cross (BbRr x BbRr) produces four gamete types in equal frequencies: BR, Br, bR, br
Punnett squares model gamete combinations resulting from meiotic segregation
Probability multiplication rule: P(two recessive alleles) = 1/2 x 1/2 = 1/4
Test crosses use homozygous recessive individuals to reveal unknown genotypes
Chromosome theory provides mechanistic explanation for Mendel's descriptive laws
examTips: FRQ alert: always explain WHY alleles segregate by citing homologous chromosome separation at anaphase I — stating the Law of Segregation alone earns no mechanism points
For dihybrid crosses, use the product rule (multiply monohybrid probabilities) rather than drawing a 16-box Punnett square to save time and reduce errors

05.02.summary: This chapter examines inheritance patterns that deviate from Mendelian genetics, focusing on incomplete dominance, codominance, multiple alleles, and pleiotropy. Students learn the molecular mechanisms behind each pattern and how to predict phenotypic ratios, including why heterozygotes produce 1:2:1 ratios instead of the classic 3:1.
keyConcepts: Incomplete dominance produces intermediate phenotypes due to gene dosage effects (50% functional protein in heterozygotes)
Codominance results in simultaneous, independent expression of both alleles in heterozygotes
Both incomplete dominance and codominance produce 1:2:1 phenotypic ratios in heterozygote crosses
ABO blood type uses three alleles (IA, IB, i) with both codominance and complete dominance
The ABO gene encodes a glycosyltransferase that adds sugar antigens to red blood cell surfaces
Pleiotropy occurs when a single gene product functions in multiple tissues or developmental pathways
Multiple allele systems show that dominance relationships vary depending on which alleles are paired
topics: Phenotypic ratios in modified dominance patterns
examTips: To distinguish codominance from incomplete dominance, ask: Can both original parental phenotypes be detected separately in the heterozygote? Yes = codominance (e.g., distinct white and black hairs in roan cattle); No = incomplete dominance (e.g., uniformly pink snapdragons).

Free response answers about incomplete dominance must include the molecular mechanism: heterozygotes produce only ~50% functional protein because only one allele encodes the active enzyme, creating a quantitatively distinct intermediate phenotype—stating that alleles 'blend' will not earn full credit.

05.03.summary: This chapter explains how genes located on the same chromosome violate Mendel's law of independent assortment due to physical linkage, and how crossing over during prophase I generates recombinant gametes at frequencies proportional to the distance between genes. Students learn to calculate recombination frequency, convert it to map distances in centimorgans, and apply chi-square analysis to determine whether observed offspring ratios indicate linkage or independent assortment.
keyConcepts: Linked genes on the same chromosome tend to be inherited together, violating independent assortment
Parental-type gametes reflect original allele combinations; recombinant-type gametes result from crossing over
Crossing over occurs during prophase I via synapsis, chiasmata formation, and strand exchange between non-sister chromatids
Only two of four chromatids in a bivalent are affected per crossover event, capping recombinant gametes at 50%
Recombination frequency (%) = (recombinant offspring / total offspring) × 100
One centimorgan (cM) equals 1% recombination frequency
Map distances are additive for genes in linear sequence on the same chromosome
Chi-square analysis determines whether deviations from expected Mendelian ratios indicate gene linkage
Cis configuration (coupling): both dominant alleles on the same chromosome (AB/ab)
Testcross design is required to accurately measure recombination frequency
topics: Linked genes and violations of independent assortment
Crossing over mechanism and recombinant gamete formation
Centimorgan units and genetic map distance
Chi-square analysis of linked vs. unlinked genes
examTips: When a dihybrid testcross ratio deviates from 1:1:1:1 with an excess of parental types, suspect gene linkage rather than a calculation error — linked genes always overproduce parental-type offspring.

Remember that crossing over affects only 2 of 4 chromatids per bivalent, so even if crossing over occurs in 100% of meioses, the maximum recombinant gamete frequency is 50%, making genes >50 cM apart appear unlinked.

05.04.summary: This chapter covers sex determination in mammals via the SRY gene and sex chromosomes, explaining how the hemizygous state of males drives X-linked inheritance patterns. Students learn to analyze pedigrees for X-linked recessive and dominant traits, apply Punnett squares with correct genotype notation, and understand X-inactivation as a mechanism producing mosaic phenotypes in heterozygous females.
keyConcepts: Sex chromosomes (XX female, XY male) and SRY gene as master regulator of male development
Hemizygosity: males carry only one allele for most X-linked genes, so recessive alleles are always expressed
X-linked recessive inheritance: trait predominantly affects males; carrier females are unaffected
Criss-cross inheritance pattern: trait passes from affected grandfather through carrier daughter to affected grandson
Obligate carrier: female deduced to carry X-linked recessive allele based on pedigree logic
X-linked dominant inheritance: affected fathers pass trait to ALL daughters and NO sons
X-inactivation (Lyon hypothesis): random inactivation of one X chromosome in each somatic cell producing mosaic phenotypes
Pseudoautosomal regions: homologous X and Y tips that allow crossing over during male meiosis
Pedigree analysis rules for distinguishing autosomal vs. X-linked and dominant vs. recessive inheritance
topics: Sex chromosome structure and gene content (X vs. Y)
SRY gene and male developmental pathway
Sperm sex chromosome segregation and sex determination ratios
Genotype notation for X-linked traits (X^H X^h notation)
Systematic pedigree analysis to distinguish inheritance modes
Mosaic phenotypes in heterozygous females (e.g., calico cats)
examTips: If a pedigree shows father-to-son transmission of a trait, immediately eliminate X-linked inheritance — sons receive the Y from dad, so any X-linked allele must come from mom.

Distinguish X-linked recessive from autosomal recessive by checking the sex ratio of affected individuals: if all or nearly all affected individuals are male, X-linked recessive is strongly indicated, whereas autosomal recessive affects both sexes equally.

05.05.summary: This chapter teaches systematic pedigree analysis for diagnosing the four Mendelian inheritance patterns—autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X-linked dominant, and X-linked recessive—using a three-filter elimination approach. It also covers conditional probability calculations for carrier frequency among unaffected individuals, a frequently tested AP Biology skill.
keyConcepts: Autosomal dominant inheritance: trait appears every generation, no skipping, both sexes equally affected
Autosomal recessive inheritance: generation skipping, carrier parents unaffected, both sexes equally affected
X-linked recessive inheritance: hemizygous males predominantly affected, carrier females unaffected
X-linked dominant inheritance: affected fathers pass trait to all daughters but no sons
Three-filter elimination system: generation skipping, sex ratio, parent-to-child transmission direction
Conditional probability: P(carrier | unaffected) = 2/3 for unaffected sibling of affected child from two carrier parents
Obligate carrier: genotype proven by pedigree transmission evidence
Hemizygosity: males have only one allele for X-linked genes, explaining male predominance in X-linked recessive conditions
Generation skipping as diagnostic evidence for recessive inheritance
Differential diagnosis: systematically eliminating inconsistent inheritance patterns
examTips: Always eliminate inheritance patterns explicitly on free response questions by citing specific pedigree individuals and mechanistic reasoning—rubrics reward elimination logic, not just pattern identification.

When calculating carrier probability for an unaffected sibling of an affected child (both parents carriers), the answer is 2/3 not 1/2—you must condition on the unaffected phenotype by removing the aa genotype from the sample space.

05.06.summary: This chapter explains how nondisjunction during meiosis I or meiosis II produces gametes with abnormal chromosome numbers, and how these errors lead to aneuploid conditions such as Down syndrome, Turner syndrome, and Klinefelter syndrome. It also introduces chromosomal structural mutations as distinct from numerical mutations, emphasizing backward reasoning from offspring genotype to meiotic error for exam success.
keyConcepts: Nondisjunction in meiosis I produces 4 abnormal gametes (2 n+1 and 2 n-1); all gametes are abnormal
Nondisjunction in meiosis II produces 2 abnormal gametes and 2 normal gametes; only one cell is affected
Aneuploidy arises when abnormal gametes participate in fertilization, producing trisomy (2n+1) or monosomy (2n-1)
Trisomy 21 (Down syndrome) results primarily from maternal meiosis I nondisjunction; frequency increases with maternal age
Turner syndrome (45,X) is monosomy of the sex chromosome; survivable due to X inactivation
Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY) results from an extra X chromosome; Y determines male development
Autosomal monosomies are nearly always lethal; autosomal trisomies for large chromosomes are also lethal
Chromosomal structural mutations (deletions, duplications, inversions, translocations) alter chromosome architecture without changing total chromosome number
Gene dosage effects explain phenotypic consequences of aneuploidy
topics: Nondisjunction mechanism in meiosis I vs. meiosis II
Gamete ratios from meiosis I vs. meiosis II nondisjunction
Backward reasoning from offspring genotype to meiotic error
examTips: If any normal gametes are produced by the affected parent, nondisjunction must have occurred in meiosis II; if all gametes are abnormal, it occurred in meiosis I — use this to eliminate answer choices on FRQs.
For origin-of-error questions (e.g., XXY Klinefelter with paternal extra X), trace backward: XY sperm can only come from meiosis I nondisjunction where X and Y homologs failed to separate.

05.07.summary: This chapter explains epigenetic mechanisms—DNA methylation and histone modification—that regulate gene expression without altering DNA sequence. It distinguishes between mitotic inheritance of epigenetic marks within an organism and transgenerational inheritance across generations, emphasizing reversibility and environmental responsiveness.
keyConcepts: DNA methylation at CpG dinucleotides silences genes by recruiting MBD proteins that block transcriptional machinery
DNA methyltransferases (DNMTs) catalyze methylation; DNMT1 maintains patterns during replication
TET enzymes actively demethylate cytosines, enabling reversibility and cellular plasticity
Histone acetylation by HATs neutralizes positive lysine charges, relaxing chromatin into euchromatin for transcription
Histone deacetylases (HDACs) remove acetyl groups, restoring positive charge and compacting chromatin into heterochromatin
Histone code: combinations of modifications (methylation, acetylation, phosphorylation) specify transcriptional outcomes
Mitotic inheritance: epigenetic marks passed to daughter cells within one organism via DNMT1 on hemimethylated DNA
Transgenerational inheritance: epigenetic marks that survive germ line reprogramming and are passed to offspring
Epigenetic changes are reversible, distinguishing them from permanent mutations
topics: DNA methylation mechanism and CpG sites
examTips: Methylation does NOT change the DNA sequence—cytosine remains cytosine; silencing occurs through MBD protein recruitment and chromatin condensation, not sequence alteration. Methylated and unmethylated genes are genetically identical.

If HDACs are inhibited, acetyl groups cannot be removed, chromatin stays open (euchromatin), and normally silenced genes remain active—trace the charge mechanism: acetylation neutralizes positive lysine, reducing attraction to negative DNA phosphates.

05.08.summary: This chapter explains how multiple genes with additive effects produce continuous phenotypic distributions (polygenic inheritance), contrasting with discrete Mendelian patterns. It covers heritability (h²) as a population-specific variance ratio, norms of reaction for genotype-environment interactions, and methods for partitioning genetic versus environmental contributions to trait variation.
keyConcepts: Polygenic inheritance and additive allelic effects
Continuous variation and bell-curve phenotypic distributions
Heritability (h²) = VG/VP as a population-specific measure
Genetic variance (VG) vs. environmental variance (VE)
Phenotypic variance = VG + VE + VG×E
Norms of reaction: one genotype expressing multiple phenotypes across environments
Twin studies for estimating heritability
Central limit theorem applied to polygenic traits
Population specificity of heritability estimates
examTips: On histogram questions, discrete bars with gaps = single-gene inheritance; smooth bell curve = polygenic inheritance. Do not confuse multiple alleles at one locus (ABO blood type, still discrete) with multiple genes (continuous distribution).

Heritability of 0.7 does NOT mean 70% of a trait is 'caused by genes' in an individual — it means 70% of phenotypic differences among individuals in that specific population are attributable to genetic differences. Heritability is always population- and environment-specific.

06.01.summary: This chapter covers the molecular machinery and chemistry of DNA replication in bacteria, focusing on the roles of helicase, SSBs, topoisomerase, primase, DNA polymerase III, DNA polymerase I, and ligase at the replication fork. It explains why DNA polymerase can only synthesize 5' to 3' and how this chemical constraint drives the asymmetry between leading and lagging strand synthesis, as well as how proofreading and mismatch repair minimize errors.
keyConcepts: Origins of replication and replication fork formation
Helicase unwinds DNA using ATP hydrolysis by breaking hydrogen bonds
Single-strand binding proteins (SSBs) prevent re-annealing and secondary structures
Topoisomerase (DNA gyrase) relieves positive supercoiling ahead of the fork by breaking and rejoining phosphodiester bonds
5' to 3' directionality of DNA synthesis due to nucleophilic attack of 3'-OH on incoming dNTP alpha phosphate
Pyrophosphate release as the energy driver for phosphodiester bond formation
Antiparallel template strands necessitate leading and lagging strand synthesis
Lagging strand synthesized discontinuously as Okazaki fragments
Sequential roles: helicase → primase → DNA Pol III → DNA Pol I → ligase
Proofreading by DNA polymerase 3' to 5' exonuclease activity
Mismatch repair as a post-replication error correction mechanism
topics: Leading strand vs. lagging strand synthesis
examTips: Helicase breaks hydrogen bonds between bases; topoisomerase breaks covalent phosphodiester bonds in the backbone to relieve supercoiling — never confuse these two on MCQ or FRQ.

On FRQ, explaining lagging strand discontinuity requires stating that DNA polymerase can only add to a 3'-OH synthesizing 5' to 3', forcing synthesis away from the fork — simply saying 'opposite direction' earns no mechanism points.

06.02.summary: This chapter covers the molecular mechanisms of transcription, from promoter recognition and initiation complex assembly in prokaryotes and eukaryotes to the distinction between template and coding strands. It also addresses eukaryotic post-transcriptional RNA processing modifications and how mutations in these systems alter gene expression.
keyConcepts: Promoter recognition by sigma factor (prokaryotes) vs. general transcription factors (eukaryotes)
TATA box and TATAAA consensus sequence recognized by TATA-binding protein (TBP)
Transcription initiation complex assembly: TFIID, TFIIB, TFIIF, TFIIE, TFIIH, and RNA polymerase II
TFIIH helicase and kinase activities required for DNA unwinding and promoter escape
Template strand (antisense, 3'→5') vs. coding strand (sense, 5'→3')
mRNA sequence is identical to coding strand with U substituted for T
RNA polymerase reads template strand 3'→5' and synthesizes mRNA 5'→3'
Post-transcriptional modifications: 5' cap, poly-A tail, and splicing of introns
Sigma factor recognition of −10 (TATAAT) and −35 (TTGACA) boxes in prokaryotes
Transcription start site (+1) is distinct from the promoter sequence
examTips: RNA polymerase reads the template strand (3'→5'); the mRNA matches the coding strand (replace T with U) — these are two different questions requiring different answers.

If TFIIH is nonfunctional, DNA cannot be unwound and RNA polymerase II cannot be phosphorylated for promoter escape, halting eukaryotic transcription; prokaryotes lack general transcription factors entirely.

06.03.summary: This chapter explains how mRNA is decoded into protein through translation, covering the role of tRNA as an adaptor molecule, ribosome structure and the A-P-E site cycle, and the three phases of translation (initiation, elongation, termination). It also addresses the genetic code's redundancy and how different mutation types affect protein structure.
keyConcepts: tRNA as adaptor molecule bridging mRNA codons and amino acids
Aminoacyl tRNA synthetase charging reaction and specificity
Anticodon-codon antiparallel base pairing and directionality
Wobble hypothesis and inosine base pairing at third codon position
Ribosomal A site (aminoacyl), P site (peptidyl), and E site (exit) functions
Peptidyl transferase activity residing in rRNA, making ribosome a ribozyme
Translocation powered by EF-G/GTP hydrolysis
Prokaryotic initiation via Shine-Dalgarno sequence
Eukaryotic cap-dependent scanning and Kozak sequence
Initiator tRNA entering P site directly (unique to initiation)
Frameshift vs. point mutations and their consequences on protein
Genetic code redundancy buffering against deleterious mutations
topics: Wobble position and synonymous codon recognition
Translation initiation in prokaryotes vs. eukaryotes
Mutation types and effects on protein structure
examTips: When reporting an anticodon, always specify directionality: if mRNA codon is 5'-CGU-3', the anticodon pairs as 3'-GCA-5', but written in standard 5'-to-3' notation it is 5'-ACG-3'; omitting direction markers will cost points on FRQs.

For FRQs tracing an amino acid through the ribosome, remember the order: charged tRNA enters A site → peptide bond transfers chain to A site tRNA → translocation moves it to P site (holding chain) → next translocation moves empty tRNA to E site → tRNA exits; the polypeptide chain never occupies the E site.
