keyConcepts: Point mutations: missense, nonsense, and silent substitutions
Codon degeneracy and the wobble position
Frameshift mutations from non-triplet insertions or deletions
Premature stop codons and truncated proteins
Nonsense-mediated decay surveillance mechanism
Silent mutations disrupting splice site consensus sequences
Base excision repair and nucleotide excision repair
Complementary strand as template for DNA repair
Repair pathway defects and cancer susceptibility
Sickle cell disease as a missense mutation example
examTips: Never conclude that a silent mutation is harmless without checking its location—if it is near an exon-intron boundary, it may disrupt splicing and produce a nonfunctional protein even though the amino acid sequence is unchanged.

Insertions or deletions of exactly three nucleotides (or multiples of three) preserve the reading frame and add/remove one amino acid rather than scrambling all downstream codons—a key exception the AP exam tests repeatedly.
06.04.summary: This chapter covers the molecular mechanisms and functional consequences of point mutations (missense, nonsense, and silent) and frameshift mutations, tracing their effects from DNA through transcription, RNA processing, and translation to the final protein. It also explains how base excision repair and nucleotide excision repair restore DNA integrity using the complementary strand as a template, and connects defects in these repair pathways to increased mutation rates and cancer susceptibility.

06.05.summary: This chapter explains the operon model of prokaryotic gene regulation, focusing on how structural components like the promoter, operator, and regulatory genes work together to coordinate gene expression. It uses the lac and trp operons as model systems to illustrate inducible versus repressible regulation, negative versus positive control, and how bacteria efficiently respond to environmental nutrient availability.
keyConcepts: Operon structure: promoter, operator, structural genes, regulatory gene
Polycistronic mRNA and coordinated gene expression
Negative regulation by repressor proteins via steric hindrance at the operator
Inducible operons: lac operon as the model system
Allolactose (not lactose) as the true inducer of the lac operon
Repressible operons: trp operon as the model system
Positive regulation by CAP-cAMP complex at the lac operon
Dual regulation of lac operon by glucose and lactose availability
Conformational changes in allosteric regulatory proteins
Effects of mutations in operon components on gene expression
topics: Logic of coordinated gene control in prokaryotes
CAP-cAMP positive regulation of the lac operon
Glucose vs. lactose availability and transcription prediction
Prokaryotic vs. eukaryotic gene expression differences
examTips: The inducer of the lac operon is allolactose, NOT lactose itself — allolactose is the isomer formed inside the cell by beta-galactosidase that binds the repressor; stating lactose will cost points on FRQs.

Prokaryotic operons produce polycistronic mRNA (multiple proteins per transcript), while eukaryotes produce monocistronic mRNA — this distinction is a frequent AP exam question about differences in gene expression.

06.06.summary: This chapter examines the multiple layers of eukaryotic gene regulation from chromatin remodeling through translation, explaining how histone modifications, transcription factors, and post-transcriptional mechanisms collectively control which genes are expressed. Students learn to apply a six-layer regulatory model to explain differential gene expression across differentiated cell types.
keyConcepts: Nucleosome structure: 147 bp DNA wrapped around histone octamer
Histone acetylation (HATs) neutralizes lysine charge → open chromatin (euchromatin) → transcription ON
Histone deacetylation (HDACs) restores lysine charge → condensed chromatin (heterochromatin) → transcription OFF
DNA methylation at CpG dinucleotides → gene silencing, heritable through cell division
Promoters vs. enhancers in transcriptional control
Combinatorial control by transcription factors
Alternative splicing as post-transcriptional regulation
miRNA and siRNA-mediated regulation of protein output
Six-layer model of eukaryotic gene regulation
Differential gene expression in differentiated cell types
examTips: Distinguish histone acetylation (opens chromatin, promotes transcription) from DNA methylation (silences genes long-term); both are epigenetic but have opposite effects—acetylation removes positive charge on histones while methylation recruits condensing proteins.

If an FRQ gives data showing normal mRNA levels but reduced protein output, target post-transcriptional or translational regulation (miRNA, siRNA, or translation inhibition), not chromatin or transcriptional layers.

06.07.summary: This chapter covers three core biotechnology techniques—PCR, gel electrophoresis, and recombinant DNA cloning—explaining the molecular mechanisms behind each. Students learn how temperature-dependent DNA chemistry enables exponential amplification, how charge and gel matrix properties separate fragments by size, and how restriction enzymes and DNA ligase enable insertion of foreign DNA into plasmid vectors.
keyConcepts: PCR thermal cycling: denaturation (95°C), annealing (50–65°C), extension (72°C)
Exponential amplification: 2^n copies after n cycles
Taq polymerase requires free 3′ OH from primer to initiate synthesis
Hydrogen bonds broken during denaturation; covalent phosphodiester bonds remain intact
DNA migrates toward positive electrode (anode) due to negative phosphate charges
Smaller fragments migrate farther in gel; larger fragments migrate less
Logarithmic relationship between fragment size and migration distance
DNA ladder used as size reference in gel electrophoresis
Restriction endonucleases cleave DNA at specific recognition sequences
Sticky ends created by restriction enzyme cuts enable compatible fragment joining
Hydrogen bonds hold sticky ends together; DNA ligase forms covalent phosphodiester bonds
Plasmid vectors carry foreign DNA inserts for recombinant DNA cloning
topics: Band interpretation and DNA ladder use
examTips: If primers are absent, incorrectly designed, or bind within (not flanking) the target, the result is zero copies—not reduced copies—because Taq polymerase cannot initiate without a primer providing a free 3′ OH group.

When interpreting gel images, locate the wells first (larger fragments stay near wells) and use the DNA ladder to orient the gel; bands farther from the wells are smaller fragments migrating toward the positive electrode.

06.08.summary: This chapter explains the molecular mechanisms of the CRISPR-Cas9 gene editing system, including how guide RNA and Cas9 work together to create targeted double-strand breaks. It then connects the two cellular DNA repair pathways—NHEJ and HDR—to specific experimental and therapeutic outcomes in biomedical and agricultural contexts.
keyConcepts: CRISPR-Cas9 two-component system (gRNA + Cas9)
Guide RNA base pairing and target specificity
Cas9 endonuclease and double-strand break creation
PAM sequence (NGG) as a binding requirement
Non-Homologous End Joining (NHEJ) and indel formation
Homology-Directed Repair (HDR) and precise editing
Frameshift mutations leading to gene knockout
Donor template requirement for HDR
Cell cycle dependence of HDR (S and G2 phases)
Somatic vs. germline editing and heritability
Off-target effects and ethical considerations
Biomedical applications: sickle cell disease, beta-thalassemia
Agricultural applications of CRISPR
topics: Germline vs. somatic cell editing ethics
examTips: Remember that guide RNA only targets (no catalytic activity) and Cas9 only cuts—changing gRNA sequence affects targeting specificity, not cutting efficiency; Cas9 mutations affect cutting, not recognition.
No donor template in an experiment = NHEJ = indels = frameshift = gene knockout; a donor template = HDR = precise correction or insertion—the AP exam tests this logic chain directly.

07.01.summary: This chapter explains Darwin's four postulates as a linked causal chain—variation, heritability, differential reproduction, and allele frequency change—that together produce evolution by natural selection. It also distinguishes heritable genetic variation from acquired characteristics, defines biological fitness strictly as reproductive success, and requires all four conditions to be present for natural selection to operate.
keyConcepts: Darwin's four postulates as a causal chain
Heritable variation vs. acquired characteristics
Lamarck's inheritance of acquired characteristics (disproven)
Central dogma and why environmental changes cannot alter germline DNA
Biological fitness as reproductive success (not physical strength)
Allele frequency change as the definition of evolution
Natural selection acts on phenotypes; evolution is measured in allele frequencies
Mutations are random with respect to fitness
Sources of heritable variation: mutation, independent assortment, crossing over
Populations evolve; individuals do not
examTips: Free response answers must explicitly connect heritable variation → differential reproduction → allele frequency change; vague claims that a trait was 'beneficial' or organisms 'adapted' earn zero points.

When a scenario involves environmental stress (e.g., antibiotic exposure), resistant variants must already exist in the population before the stress—the stress selects for pre-existing variants, it does not cause resistance to arise.

07.02.summary: This chapter introduces Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium as a null model in population genetics, explaining the mathematical framework (p+q=1 and p²+2pq+q²=1) used to predict genotype frequencies from allele frequencies. Students learn to calculate allele and genotype frequencies from phenotype data, identify the five conditions required for equilibrium, and apply deviations from expected frequencies as evidence of evolutionary forces.
keyConcepts: Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium as a null model for detecting evolutionary change
p + q = 1 (allele frequency equation)
p² + 2pq + q² = 1 (genotype frequency equation)
Five conditions for Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium: large population, random mating, no mutation, no migration, no natural selection
Evolution defined as change in allele frequencies over time
Distinction between allele frequencies and genotype frequencies
Entry point for calculations: q² from recessive phenotype data
Excess homozygosity as a signal of non-random mating (inbreeding)
Genetic drift as cause of erratic frequency fluctuations in small populations
Matching H-W predictions means data are consistent with null hypothesis, not proof of no evolution
topics: Detecting evolutionary forces via H-W deviations
examTips: Always start Hardy-Weinberg calculations with q² (recessive phenotype count ÷ total population), then find q, then p, then compute p², 2pq; verify all three genotype frequencies sum to exactly 1.

Never omit the coefficient 2 in the heterozygote term (2pq); also remember that data matching H-W predictions does not prove evolution is absent—it only means the data are consistent with the null hypothesis.

07.03.summary: This chapter examines the three modes of natural selection—directional, stabilizing, and disruptive—by analyzing how each reshapes the mean and variance of phenotype distributions over generations. Students learn to interpret graphical representations of selection, connect these mechanisms to real examples like peppered moths and human birth weight, and link disruptive selection to sympatric speciation.
keyConcepts: Phenotype distribution (mean and variance as targets of selection)
Directional selection shifts the mean toward one extreme phenotype
Stabilizing selection maintains the mean while reducing variance
Disruptive selection favors both extremes over intermediates, increasing variance
Industrial melanism as evidence of directional selection
Human birth weight as evidence of stabilizing selection
Disruptive selection as a mechanism for sympatric speciation
Fitness landscapes and differential reproductive success
Allele frequency change as the genetic basis of selection
Phenotypic stasis as a result of long-term stabilizing selection
topics: Stabilizing selection and optimal intermediate phenotypes
examTips: When analyzing before/after distribution graphs, always check two things independently: did the peak position (mean) shift, and did the curve width (variance) change—a narrower curve with the same peak is stabilizing, not directional selection.

In free response, directional selection answers must name the favored phenotype, explain why it has higher fitness in the specific environment, describe how allele frequencies shift, and state that the mean moves toward the favored extreme—stating only that the environment changed is insufficient for full credit.

07.04.summary: This chapter explains how genetic drift and gene flow change allele frequencies in populations independently of natural selection, with drift driven by random sampling error (especially in small populations) and gene flow driven by migration of individuals between populations. It covers the bottleneck and founder effects as specific causes of drift, and analyzes how these mechanisms interact with natural selection to shape population genetics.
keyConcepts: Genetic drift as random sampling error, not differential fitness
Allele fixation and loss through drift
Effective population size and its relationship to drift strength
Bottleneck effect: catastrophic population size reduction in place
Founder effect: small group migrates to establish new colony
Mutational meltdown in small populations
Gene flow as transfer of alleles via migration or gamete movement
Homogenization of allele frequencies through gene flow
Gene flow counteracting local adaptation by natural selection
Ellis van Creveld syndrome as a founder effect example
Northern elephant seal as a bottleneck effect example
topics: Interactions between drift, gene flow, and natural selection
examTips: If a harmful or neutral allele increases in frequency in a small or isolated population, genetic drift is almost certainly the correct mechanism—natural selection would decrease harmful alleles, not increase them.

To distinguish bottleneck from founder effect, look for geography and cause: bottleneck = population reduced in place by catastrophe; founder effect = small group migrates to establish a new population elsewhere.

07.05.summary: This chapter examines sexual selection through intrasexual and intersexual mechanisms, explaining how costly traits can evolve when mating advantages outweigh survival costs via the handicap principle and runaway selection. It also analyzes how non-random mating violates Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium by shifting genotype frequencies while leaving allele frequencies unchanged in the absence of other evolutionary forces.
keyConcepts: Intrasexual selection: same-sex competition determines mating access (e.g., elk antlers)
Intersexual selection: one sex chooses mates based on preferred traits (e.g., peacock tails)
Identifying the selecting agent to distinguish intrasexual vs. intersexual selection
Survival-reproduction tradeoff: mating advantages can compensate for survival costs
Handicap principle: costly traits as honest signals of genetic quality
Fisher's runaway selection: genetically correlated trait-preference co-evolution
Non-random mating changes genotype frequencies but not allele frequencies
Hardy-Weinberg condition of random mating violated by sexual selection
topics: Costly trait evolution and the peacock paradox
Runaway selection and positive feedback loops
Genotype frequency vs. allele frequency changes
examTips: To classify a behavior as intrasexual or intersexual selection, identify the selecting agent: if females choose among displaying males it is intersexual; if male-vs-male combat determines the winner regardless of female preference it is intrasexual.

When asked why a survival-reducing trait spreads, explicitly state that fitness equals total reproductive output—mating advantages must be shown to outweigh survival costs so carriers produce more offspring despite dying younger; simply labeling it 'sexually selected' is insufficient for FRQ credit.

07.06.summary: This chapter explains how new species form through allopatric and sympatric speciation, emphasizing that true speciation requires intrinsic reproductive isolation rather than mere geographic separation. It covers the biological species concept, reproductive isolating mechanisms (prezygotic and postzygotic), polyploidy, and adaptive radiation.
keyConcepts: Biological species concept: interbreeding to produce viable, fertile offspring
Reproductive isolation as the defining criterion for speciation
Gene flow and its role in maintaining genetic cohesion
Allopatric speciation via geographic barriers
Sympatric speciation without geographic separation
Polyploidy (autopolyploidy and allopolyploidy) as a mechanism of instant speciation
Prezygotic barriers: habitat, temporal, behavioral, mechanical, gametic isolation
Postzygotic barriers: reduced hybrid viability or fertility
Adaptive radiation driven by geographic isolation and ecological opportunity
Chromosome number compatibility and meiotic pairing in hybridization
topics: Evidence for speciation in isolated populations
examTips: On FRQs, always tie speciation to reproductive isolation, not just geographic separation—state that populations must be unable to produce viable, fertile offspring even if the barrier were removed.

For multiple choice, distinguish allopatric from sympatric speciation by how reproductive isolation arises (geographic isolation first vs. direct mechanisms like polyploidy), not by where populations currently live.

keyConcepts: Cladograms show branching relationships, not evolutionary progress or ranking
Nodes represent common ancestors; terminal taxa all exist in the present
Topology can be rotated at any node without changing evolutionary meaning
Clades (monophyletic groups) include an ancestor and ALL of its descendants
Synapomorphies (shared derived characters) define clades
Plesiomorphies (ancestral characters) cannot define more recent clades
Outgroups are used to distinguish ancestral from derived character states
Paraphyletic groups are invalid because they exclude some descendants
Homologous structures share a common ancestor and structural blueprint
Analogous structures share function but arose through convergent evolution
Molecular clocks use mutation rates to estimate divergence times
Conflicts between morphological and molecular data can challenge phylogenetic hypotheses
topics: Molecular clocks and divergence time estimation
examTips: Never equate left-to-right position on a cladogram with evolutionary advancement; all terminal taxa have evolved equally long since their common ancestor
When identifying a synapomorphy for a clade, always verify the trait is absent in the outgroup — if the outgroup shares it, the character is ancestral and cannot define the clade
07.07.summary: This chapter teaches students how to correctly read cladograms as maps of shared ancestry rather than rankings of evolutionary progress, and how to identify valid clades using shared derived characters (synapomorphies). It also covers distinguishing homologous from analogous structures, applying molecular clock data to estimate divergence times, and resolving conflicts between morphological and molecular phylogenetic evidence.

07.08.summary: This chapter examines the multiple independent lines of evidence supporting evolutionary theory, including the fossil record, comparative anatomy, molecular phylogenetics, and biogeography. Students learn to distinguish homologous from analogous structures, interpret transitional fossils and stratigraphic sequences, and understand how converging evidence from different fields strengthens evolutionary hypotheses.
keyConcepts: Stratigraphic sequencing as temporal evidence for evolution
Transitional fossils and intermediate morphology
Fossilization bias and incompleteness of the fossil record
Homologous structures indicating common ancestry
Analogous structures and convergent evolution
Vestigial structures as evidence of descent with modification
Molecular phylogenetics using DNA and protein sequences
Biogeographic distribution patterns and common ancestry
Divergent evolution
Multiple independent lines of evidence corroborating evolutionary relationships
topics: Tiktaalik as a transitional fossil example
examTips: Never claim the fossil record is complete on the AP exam; explain fossilization bias and state that gaps reflect preservation probability, not evolutionary absence.

To distinguish homology from analogy, focus on underlying anatomical structure (same bones, same arrangement = homology) rather than function; analogous structures share function but differ in structural organization.

08.01.summary: This chapter covers population ecology by comparing exponential and logistic growth models, explaining how the (K-N)/K term creates density-dependent negative feedback as populations approach carrying capacity. It also distinguishes density-dependent from density-independent limiting factors and examines life history tradeoffs between r-selected and K-selected reproductive strategies.
keyConcepts: Exponential growth equation: dN/dt = rN
Intrinsic rate of natural increase (r = b - d)
Doubling time: ln(2)/r
Logistic growth equation: dN/dt = rN(K-N)/K
Carrying capacity (K)
The (K-N)/K braking term and negative feedback
Inflection point at N = K/2
Sigmoid (S-shaped) growth curve
Maximum sustainable yield at N = K/2
Density-dependent limiting factors (competition, disease, predation)
Density-independent limiting factors
r-selected vs. K-selected life history strategies
topics: Life history tradeoffs and reproductive strategies
examTips: Increasing doubling times as a population grows signals logistic growth, not exponential, because per capita growth rate is declining.
Logistic and exponential growth are not sequential phases—if a population eventually plateaus, the entire trajectory is logistic; exponential growth by definition never levels off.

08.02.summary: This chapter covers the classification and mechanisms of ecological interactions—predation, parasitism, competition, mutualism, and commensalism—by evaluating measurable fitness effects on both species involved. It also examines competitive exclusion, character displacement, niche partitioning, and the disproportionate role of keystone species in shaping community structure.
keyConcepts: Ecological interaction classification by fitness effect (+/−/0) on both species
Predation (+/−) vs. parasitism (+/−): mechanism and duration distinctions
Competition (−/−): interspecific vs. intraspecific
Competitive exclusion principle (Gause's principle)
Character displacement as evolutionary response to competition
Niche partitioning as ecological outcome enabling coexistence
Mutualism (+/+) vs. commensalism (+/0)
Mycorrhizal associations and nitrogen-fixing bacteria as obligate mutualisms
Keystone species and trophic cascades
Food web dynamics and community stability
topics: Niche partitioning in MacArthur's warblers and Anolis lizards
Keystone species effects on community structure
Trophic cascades from keystone species removal or addition
examTips: Always state the fitness effect on Species A and Species B separately before naming the interaction type; AP rubrics require justification for both participants.

When two similar species coexist, explain coexistence by identifying the specific resource dimension (spatial, temporal, morphological) along which niche partitioning occurs—not just that the species differ.

08.03.summary: This chapter covers ecosystem energy flow, beginning with the distinction between GPP and NPP, then tracing the three fates of consumed energy across trophic levels to explain why ecological efficiency averages only 10%. It also addresses how endothermy versus ectothermy affects production efficiency and how food web structure determines ecosystem stability.
keyConcepts: NPP = GPP − Respiration; NPP is the only energy available to consumers
Three fates of consumed energy: feces (detrital chain), cellular respiration (heat loss), biomass (available to next trophic level)
Ecological efficiency = energy at higher trophic level ÷ energy at lower trophic level (ranges 5–20%, not always 10%)
Assimilation efficiency varies with diet: low in herbivores (~30%), high in carnivores (~80%)
Production efficiency is higher in ectotherms than endotherms due to lower thermoregulation costs
Endotherms lose 80%+ of assimilated energy to respiration for thermoregulation
Food webs vs. food chains: webs show realistic interconnections; species removal can cascade through multiple trophic levels
Trophic levels: producers (1) → primary consumers (2) → secondary consumers (3) → tertiary consumers (4)
topics: Energy loss as heat (second law of thermodynamics)
examTips: Always use NPP (not GPP) as the energy available to consumers; subtract producer respiration before any calculation.
When a question provides actual energy values at each trophic level, calculate ecological efficiency from the data (higher ÷ lower) rather than automatically applying the 10% rule.

08.04.summary: This chapter examines the carbon, nitrogen, and phosphorus biogeochemical cycles, detailing the mechanisms by which each element moves between atmospheric, biological, and geological reservoirs. It emphasizes bacterial roles as rate-limiting steps in the nitrogen cycle, the absence of an atmospheric phosphorus reservoir, and how human disruptions to these cycles lead to consequences such as eutrophication.
keyConcepts: Carbon fixation via RuBisCO in the Calvin cycle
Cellular respiration releases CO2 in both plants and animals
Decomposition returns carbon to atmosphere via extracellular enzyme breakdown
Fossil fuel combustion releases geologically sequestered carbon
Nitrogen fixation by prokaryotes (Rhizobium, Azotobacter) as the rate-limiting bottleneck
Nitrification: Nitrosomonas converts NH3 to NO2-, Nitrobacter converts NO2- to NO3-
Denitrification returns N2 to atmosphere under anaerobic conditions
Ammonification recycles nitrogen from decomposing organic matter
Assimilation incorporates nitrate into amino acids via nitrate reductase
Nitrogenase is oxygen-sensitive and requires 16 ATP per N2 fixed
Phosphorus cycle lacks an atmospheric reservoir, making it vulnerable to depletion
Eutrophication results from nutrient overload disrupting aquatic ecosystems
topics: Photosynthesis and respiration as opposing carbon processes
Nitrogen cycle steps and bacterial transformations
Leghemoglobin and root nodule oxygen regulation
examTips: Plants both photosynthesize AND respire continuously; at night only respiration occurs, releasing CO2 — AP exams frequently test this misconception with chamber data questions.

Nitrogen fixation is the bottleneck of the entire nitrogen cycle; eliminating nitrogen-fixing bacteria halts new nitrogen input regardless of how efficiently nitrification, assimilation, or denitrification operate.

08.05.summary: This chapter covers ecological succession, distinguishing primary and secondary succession based on whether the soil biological legacy survived the disturbance. It explains the facilitation model of pioneer species, climax community dynamics, and how successional principles apply to volcanic, glacial, and anthropogenic disturbance scenarios.
keyConcepts: Primary succession occurs on substrates with no soil biological legacy; secondary succession occurs when soil infrastructure survives disturbance
Soil biological legacy includes seed banks, mycorrhizal fungi, nitrogen-fixing bacteria, root fragments, and organic matter
Facilitation model: pioneer species mechanistically modify abiotic conditions (soil formation, nutrient cycling, microclimate) to favor subsequent colonizers while reducing their own fitness
Lichens secrete organic acids (carbonic and oxalic) to chemically weather rock, producing primitive soil over centuries
Tolerance model: late-successional species dominate by tolerating lower resource availability
Inhibition model: early colonizers actively resist replacement until death or disturbance
Climax communities represent dynamic equilibria, not permanent endpoints
Disturbance regime alterations (e.g., fire suppression) can disrupt successional outcomes in fire-adapted ecosystems
topics: Volcanic, glacial, and anthropogenic disturbance scenarios
examTips: Never use disturbance severity to classify succession type — always ask whether the soil biological legacy survived; a thin ash deposit over intact soil = secondary succession, soil scoured to bedrock = primary succession

When explaining pioneer species facilitation, describe the specific mechanism (e.g., lichens secrete organic acids that weather rock, dead organic matter accumulates to form primitive soil) — vague answers about 'making conditions better' earn minimal credit

08.06.summary: This chapter examines biodiversity measurement through species richness and evenness, then applies the MacArthur-Wilson equilibrium model of island biogeography to predict species diversity based on island size and distance from mainland. It extends these principles to habitat fragmentation, population viability, and evidence-based conservation strategies including corridor design and reserve optimization.
keyConcepts: Species richness vs. species evenness
Shannon Diversity Index (H)
Functional redundancy and ecosystem resilience
MacArthur-Wilson equilibrium theory of island biogeography
Immigration rate and extinction rate curves
Equilibrium species number and species turnover
Effect of island size on extinction rate
Effect of island distance on immigration rate
Habitat fragmentation as ecological island creation
Minimum viable population (MVP)
Demographic stochasticity and genetic drift in small populations
Conservation corridor design
Reserve size optimization
topics: Shannon Diversity Index calculation and interpretation
Ranking islands by predicted species diversity
Habitat fragmentation effects on population viability
Immigration and extinction dynamics in fragmented habitats
examTips: When comparing biodiversity between two communities, always address both richness AND evenness—a community with fewer species but high evenness can have a higher Shannon Index than one with more species but extreme dominance.

When ranking islands by species diversity, analyze island size (shifts extinction curve down) and distance from mainland (shifts immigration curve up) separately before combining—large AND close islands achieve both benefits simultaneously.

keyConcepts: Greenhouse gas molecular absorption and re-emission of infrared radiation
Shortwave vs. longwave radiation and wavelength shift at Earth's surface
Radiative forcing and Earth's energy budget imbalance
Competitive release and energetic reallocation in invasive species
Trophic cascades triggered by invasive species
Sixth mass extinction and compounding anthropogenic drivers
Habitat fragmentation as primary biodiversity loss driver
Biogeochemical cycle disruption by human activity
Carbon cycle perturbation via fossil fuel combustion and deforestation
Biological control risks and invasive species management
examTips: FRQ rubrics require two distinct steps: CO2 absorbs outgoing infrared (longwave) radiation, then re-emits it in all directions including back toward Earth's surface — writing 'CO2 traps heat' earns zero mechanism points

For invasive species questions, name 'competitive release' explicitly and link it to escape from co-evolved predators, parasites, and pathogens — then trace trophic cascade effects through specific energy pathways rather than just saying invasives 'outcompete' natives
08.07.summary: This chapter examines the molecular mechanisms behind the greenhouse effect, the ecological dynamics of invasive species through competitive release and trophic cascades, and the compounding factors driving the sixth mass extinction. Students learn to connect human-caused disruptions — fossil fuel combustion, habitat loss, and biological introductions — to measurable changes in energy flow, population dynamics, and biogeochemical cycles.

08.08.summary: This chapter examines animal behavior through two complementary lenses: proximate causation (immediate hormonal, neural, and sensory mechanisms) and ultimate causation (evolutionary advantages conferred by natural selection). It covers fixed action patterns triggered by sign stimuli, imprinting during critical periods, and kin selection via Hamilton's Rule as frameworks for understanding both the mechanics and adaptive significance of behavior.
keyConcepts: Proximate vs. ultimate causation (Tinbergen's framework)
Fixed action patterns (FAPs) and sign stimuli
Innate releasing mechanism and central pattern generators
